title: Ibrahim's du'a
hook: make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer (14:40)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adam's du'a, and your line: we wronged ourselves. Did you say it was yours, before the explanation? Today, a prayer from a man at the other end of a long life. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

Ibrahim has done almost everything a person of faith could do. He broke the idols. He walked out of the fire. He left his wife and baby in an empty valley on Allah's word. With his son Isma'il, he raised the walls of the Ka'bah, stone by stone. If anyone had earned the right to feel sure of himself, it's him. And at the end of his prayer in surah fourteen, he still asks to be kept, and to be accepted.

Surah Ibrahim, verse forty, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Make me to establish proper worship, and some of my posterity (also); our Lord! and accept the prayer." Two requests. The first: make me keep up the prayer, me and my children after me. Not make me rich, not make me remembered. Keep me praying, and keep them praying. Notice he asks for himself first. Even Ibrahim doesn't assume he'll stay steady on his own. The second request is the one in today's line: wa taqabbal du'a', and accept my prayer. Just asking isn't the end of it. He asks for the asking to be received. Then, in the next verse, he widens the circle: our Lord, forgive me, and my parents, and the believers, on the day the reckoning is set up. Here's the scholar's thread. The same man says the same kind of thing in al-Baqarah, verse one twenty-seven, while the walls of the Ka'bah are going up: our Lord, accept from us. Commentators record that an early pious man, Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, wept when he recited it: the Friend of the Merciful is building Allah's own House, and he's afraid it won't be accepted. In both places, Ibrahim doesn't treat a good deed as finished just because it's done. Some Muslims recite these verses, fourteen forty and forty-one, in the last sitting of their prayer, so the prayer ends asking for itself to be accepted.

The practice: pray for your family's prayers. Sit, and bring your family to mind one by one: parents, children, siblings, a partner, whoever is yours. For each, picture them in a quiet moment of their own, praying, or just pausing, or looking for meaning in their way. If you pray, ask for each of them by name, as Ibrahim did, that they'd keep their prayer. If you don't, simply wish each of them steadiness. Then, at the end, add Ibrahim's last words: and accept my prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ibrahim's du'a. Make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer: the builder of the Ka'bah, still asking to be accepted. Today's word.
Your line: accept my prayer. Today, after you finish one good thing, don't tick it off; ask, quietly, that it be accepted. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Ibrahim's du'a (14:40–41) in the final sitting of the prayer, before the closing salam, asking for themselves, their children and their parents.

pairs: make me and my children keep the prayer
forgive me, my parents, the believers

myth: Ibrahim asked only for his children to keep the prayer
he asked for himself first: make me establish worship, and some of my offspring.
Ibrahim asked for acceptance while building the Ka'bah
Ibrahim's prayer in surah fourteen includes his parents
14:41: forgive me and my parents and the believers.

fork.setup: you've just finished building the Ka'bah with your son, at Allah's command. what do you pray?
options: make it the greatest house on earth.
fork.reveal: Ibrahim and Isma'il ask for acceptance (2:127), and commentators record that an early pious man wept at it.

original.note: Arabic, 14:40: our Lord, and accept my prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ibrahim prayed for his children.
what it means: he prayed to keep the prayer himself, then for his children, and asked for the prayer itself to be accepted.
what a scholar hears: taqabbal echoes 2:127; Ibn Kathir records Wuhayb ibn al-Ward weeping that the Friend of the Merciful feared rejection.

notes: Pickthall wording of 14:40 quoted from memory; please confirm.
